questions.prompt: Geocoding is:
choices: Assigning coordinates to data that describe a location another way, such as an address
Aligning a scanned map to coordinates
questions.explain: Address matching is the most common kind.

questions.prompt: Address matching places an address by:
choices: Comparing it with a reference file whose features carry addresses
questions.explain: The output is a point layer that keeps the original attributes.

questions.prompt: Georeferencing is:
choices: Transforming a raster from file coordinates to map coordinates
Joining a CSV to a layer
questions.explain: It is a kind of image rectification.

questions.prompt: On U.S. streets, odd house numbers are usually on one side and even numbers on the other.
questions.explain: That, plus numbers that increase along the street, is what makes interpolation possible.

questions.prompt: Which reference file gives the most accurate geocoded points?
questions.explain: A match finds the exact property.

questions.prompt: Which reference file gives the least accurate points?
questions.explain: Every address in a large region lands on one point.

questions.prompt: With five-digit ZIP Code centroids as the reference, every address in a ZIP Code is placed:
questions.explain: Fast and almost always matches, but imprecise.

questions.prompt: A ZIP+4 code identifies:
choices: A short segment of a delivery route, such as one side of a block
questions.explain: The address is placed at the segment's center.

questions.prompt: TIGER/Line street segments store:
choices: Address ranges for the left and right sides of each segment
The exact location of every house
questions.explain: Addresses are interpolated along the segment.

questions.prompt: Put the steps of street-centerline matching in order.
answer: Find the street segment by name and address range
Choose the side of the street (odd or even)
Interpolate the position along the segment
questions.explain: Query, side, then interpolation.

questions.prompt: A segment's right side holds 1101–1199, and X runs from 42 to 52. What is the interpolated X of 1147? (one decimal)
The same segment's left side holds 1100–1198. What is the interpolated X of 1184? (one decimal)
Which side of the street is 1184 on, if the left side holds 1100–1198 and the right 1101–1199?
questions.explain: 1184 is even.

questions.prompt: Linear interpolation assumes that:
choices: Addresses are spaced evenly along the segment
Every house is on a corner
Houses are numbered by construction date
questions.explain: Uneven lots or unused numbers move the true house away from the estimate.

questions.prompt: Why do geocoders move interpolated points a few meters off the centerline?
choices: So houses on opposite sides of the street don't land on the same spot
questions.explain: The offset puts each point on its own side.

questions.prompt: The Census Geocoder can match a batch of up to how many addresses?
questions.explain: It also returns the census tract, block group, and block.

questions.prompt: A match score measures:
choices: How closely an address agrees with a reference candidate
The distance to the ZIP centroid
questions.explain: Often from 0 to 100.

questions.prompt: The match rate is:
choices: The share of addresses that were matched
The score of the best candidate
questions.explain: Always report it with your results.

questions.prompt: A tied address is one that:
choices: Has two or more candidates with the same score
questions.explain: Such as Main St in two towns.

questions.prompt: Unmatched addresses are usually missing at random, so they don't bias a map.
questions.explain: Rural routes, new subdivisions, and messy entries fail more often.

questions.prompt: Address standardization:
choices: Parses addresses into parts so that 'East Franklin Street' and 'E Franklin St' match
questions.explain: It happens before matching.

questions.prompt: In a traditional Japanese address, buildings on a block were often numbered:
choices: In the order they were built
questions.explain: Which is why street interpolation doesn't work there.

questions.prompt: A scanned map's file coordinates are:
questions.explain: Georeferencing converts them to map coordinates.

questions.prompt: A ground control point (GCP) is:
choices: A feature you can find on both the image and a reference layer
questions.explain: GCPs tie the image to the map.

questions.prompt: Which makes the best ground control point?
questions.explain: Good GCPs are easy to find, accurate, and stable.

questions.prompt: GCPs should be:
choices: Spread evenly across the whole image
questions.explain: Unconstrained areas can warp badly.

questions.prompt: Put the georeferencing steps in order.
questions.explain: Know, control, transform, validate, rectify.

questions.prompt: A first-order (affine) transformation has how many coefficients?
questions.explain: a0, a1, a2 and b0, b1, b2.

questions.prompt: An affine transformation can correct all of these EXCEPT:
questions.explain: Nonlinear distortion needs a higher-order polynomial.

questions.prompt: Minimum number of GCPs for a first-order transformation?
questions.explain: Three points fix the six coefficients.

questions.prompt: Minimum number of GCPs for a second-order transformation?
questions.explain: Second order has 12 coefficients.

questions.prompt: Minimum number of GCPs for a third-order transformation?
questions.explain: Third order has 20 coefficients.

questions.prompt: Why collect more than the minimum number of GCPs?
choices: So the error can be measured
questions.explain: With exactly the minimum, the fit is perfect and the RMSE is zero.

questions.prompt: Which transformation order should you use?
choices: The lowest order that gives acceptable error
questions.explain: High orders warp areas far from the GCPs.

questions.prompt: GCP-based transformation coefficients are usually solved by:
questions.explain: It minimizes the overall error at the GCPs.

questions.prompt: A spline (rubber-sheet) transformation:
choices: Fits every GCP exactly, so the residuals are all zero
questions.explain: That hides errors at the GCPs.

questions.prompt: Which resampling method keeps the original cell values, for categorical data?
questions.explain: Use it for land cover.

questions.prompt: Cubic convolution resampling uses how many input cells?
questions.explain: Bilinear uses 4; nearest neighbor uses 1.

questions.prompt: A GCP's residual is:
choices: The distance between where the transformation puts it and where it really is
questions.explain: A large residual flags a misplaced GCP.

questions.prompt: Put the steps for computing the RMSE in order.
questions.explain: Root of the mean of the squares.

questions.prompt: Residuals of 3, 4, and 0 m. What is the RMSE, to one decimal place?
Four GCPs have squared residuals averaging 3,275.77. What is the RMSE, to one decimal place?
A common target RMSE is:
choices: Smaller than the raster's cell size
questions.explain: For 1 m air photos, under 1 m.

questions.prompt: One GCP's residual is far larger than the others. What should you do first?
choices: Check whether it was placed on the wrong feature, and fix or delete it
Add more GCPs next to it
questions.explain: Then recheck the RMSE.

questions.prompt: In ArcGIS Pro, Save (rather than Save as New) after georeferencing:
choices: Stores the transformation in an auxiliary file without changing the pixels
questions.explain: Save as New writes a rectified copy.

questions.prompt: Where is the Georeferencer in QGIS?
questions.explain: It is built in.
